sentences: In the middle of a silver-grey valley of snow, a still pool reflects the trees and the sky.
This is Winter Harmony, by the American impressionist John Henry Twachtman.
It is painted in oil on canvas, 65.4 centimetres high and 81.1 centimetres wide.
The National Gallery of Art in Washington acquired it in 1964, and the museum dates it to around 1890 to 1900.
This is the painter's own land.
Born in Cincinnati and trained in Munich and Venice, Twachtman moved his family to a farm near Greenwich, Connecticut, within reach of his teaching job in Manhattan.
Through two purchases, in 1890 and 1891, he acquired more than sixteen acres, including a rocky brook that opens into a quiet pond surrounded by hemlock trees.
Look at the pool in the centre.
He called this place the Hemlock Pool and painted it again and again.
The trees, the snow and the sky are present in the reflections just as fully as in the landscape itself.
Now look at the colour.
Over the silver-grey, subdued blues and mauves catch the fleeting changes of light on an overcast day.
The shimmering greens of the hemlock needles and the golden brown leaves still clinging to some branches are laid in with feathery touches.
His brushwork is not that of a French impressionist.
Instead of placing separate touches of colour side by side, he adapted an old master technique, scumbling nearly dry paint into overlapping layers.
He worked loosely, so the tints underneath show through the gaps in the covering strokes.
In December 1891 he wrote to his friend, the painter J.
Alden Weir, that they must have snow, and lots of it.
Nature, he felt, was never lovelier than when it was snowing, with the whole earth wrapped up and everything hushed.
This painting gathers up exactly that quiet.
It may be the picture shown as Hemlock Pool in his 1891 exhibition at the Wunderlich Gallery in New York.
Around 1900 it belonged to Mrs Lucius Horatio Biglow, who is believed to have bought it from the artist, and it came up at auction in 1963 as Winter Scene.
Its present title was given only after that sale.
Twachtman was happiest in his life and work during the Greenwich years of the 1890s, but he was never good at selling his pictures.
Fellow artists revered him as a painter's painter, and he died suddenly in 1902.
Step back and look once more.
This is the stillness left after one man looked, winter after winter, at a small pool behind his own house.
Think of a place you pass every day that deserves a longer look.
